Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has grown into one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), with a market cap of around $445 billion. But these three promising companies could exceed it over the next five years: Celestica (NYSE: CLS), CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), and AppLovin (NASDAQ: APP).

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

AI data center networking could drive Celestica's growth

Throughout the AI data center build-out, chip companies and cloud providers have gotten the lion's share of the attention. But those gigantic server clusters need more than just powerful processors and copious amounts of memory. They also require better networking hardware to move information between processors, as well as better cooling systems and more efficient racks, especially as AI systems become more complex. Those are the niches Celestica competes in, and the company's latest results show that demand is accelerating.

Celestica delivered its third-quarter results on Oct. 26, reporting revenue growth of 83% year over year and raised its full-year outlook. Looking ahead, management's 2027 outlook suggests continued growth, supported by stronger demand from major cloud customers and AI developers.

That means Celestica could eventually become more valuable than Palantir if the AI data center build-out continues expanding and the company can capture a meaningful share of that spending. Currently, its guiding for 90% revenue growth in 2027.

But to exceed Palantir's current size, Celestica would need to grow its market cap 13-fold. Meanwhile, the risk is that AI spending could weaken, supply chain issues could hurt revenue, and the company's customer concentration could cause problems down the road.

AI cybersecurity could become a major opportunity for CrowdStrike

CrowdStrike's opportunity isn't limited to traditional cybersecurity. As malicious actors use AI to power more sophisticated cyberattacks, the company could become a major security-layer provider for addressing AI-related threats.

Demand for that type of protection is already driving meaningful growth. In its 2027 fiscal second quarter, CrowdStrike reported annual recurring revenue (ARR) of around $5.8 billion, up 25% year over year, and raised its full-year net new ARR growth outlook.

title: Is Palantir Stock a Buy?
detail:
Is Palantir Stock a Buy?
Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 6:07 AM CST 4 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) is one of the most successful stocks in the AI boom, having risen by over 3,200% from its all-time low in 2022.

In recent weeks, it had pulled back before recovering some of the losses over the last few trading sessions. The question for investors is whether that pullback makes Palantir stock a buy or whether investors should stay on the sidelines. Under current conditions, I would lean toward watching Palantir instead of buying it, and here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The price of Palantir

Investors are likely wondering what to make of the price action surrounding Palantir. A pullback last week took the SaaS stock into correction territory. Nonetheless, before investors could even debate whether that correction made Palantir a buy, the stock recovered, and it's only about 7% off the all-time high it set mid-month.

To be sure, the productivity gains Palantir has delivered to its clients are probably the best argument for paying the stock's premium valuation.

For example, Wendy's solved a problem involving real-time order and inventory tracking within five minutes, a process that once took weeks. Also, with the help of Palantir and Nvidia, L3 Harris Technologies cut costs in a test environment by 95% using an internally built AI setup.

However, one has to wonder whether such successes are already reflected in the stock price. As previously mentioned, Palantir is near a record high, and analysts forecast annual revenue growth of 84% this year and 50% in 2027.

Moreover, given its valuation, such gains suggest the ability to profit from Palantir's success is uncertain at best. Its current P/E ratio stands at 166, and even when looking at the forward P/E ratio, it sells for about 121 forward earnings.

Plus, the forward one-year P/E ratio, which pertains to 2027 earnings, is at 83, suggesting its stock price is years ahead of its stock performance. The cancellation of such growth, or even its interruption, could cast doubts on its investment case, causing the stock to fall. Given that risk, investors should ponder any decisions about trading Palantir carefully.

Should investors buy Palantir stock?

Considering Palantir's valuation, investors should probably avoid buying additional shares of the stock.

Of course, Palantir has driven massive growth, as its software delivers game-changing productivity gains for clients and high-double-digit revenue growth.

Few stocks divide a room of investors quite like Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) does right now. Ask 10 people who follow the stock whether it's the most important software company of the artificial intelligence era or the most dangerous bubble on the market, and you'll get 10 equally confident, opposite answers.

Both bullish and bearish camps are working from the same facts; they just weigh them differently. So instead of picking a side, here's my actual attempt to pin down where this stock might land by the end of 2027, including bull and bear cases.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What Palantir is doing right now

Let's start with the plain fact that growth hasn't slowed down much this year. In the second quarter of 2026, Palantir's total revenue grew 93% year over year, and its U.S. commercial business, the part of the company selling to regular corporations rather than governments, grew 149% to $764 million. That's not a one-quarter fluke either; Palantir has now beaten Wall Street's earnings estimates nine straight quarters.

On the government side, the business that built Palantir's reputation, the U.S. Army expanded its Maven Smart System AI contract by $618 million in August. NATO finalized a sole-source procurement deal for the same platform this year. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to roughly $8.15 billion, implying growth of about 82% for the year.

The bull case for Palantir

If you believe in Palantir, this is why: a company growing commercial revenue by triple digits while also deepening its grip on defense and intelligence work isn't supposed to exist, and the market has rewarded that combination all year, with the stock jumping roughly 60% in the third quarter alone after a rough start to 2026.

Bulls will argue that Palantir's AIP platform created real, sticky demand that took years to build and can't be replicated overnight, and that government agencies, not just in the U.S. but in the U.K. and across NATO, are now locked into multi-year platform commitments that are hard to rip out once installed. If revenue keeps compounding anywhere close to its current pace through 2027, and the market keeps paying up for that growth the way it has, a path toward $250 per share or higher isn't a stretch.

Investors will hear from Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, this week.
Credit: Karl Mondon / AFP via Getty Images

AI drove a lot of the news cycle last week. It could do the same in the week ahead.

Investors are likely still digesting the paperwork Anthropic filed ahead of its IPO. Several tech giants reported, too, and not all of their results were well-received by investors. Now we'll be watching for insights about how AI fits into Apple's vision and broader strategy when John Ternus attends his first earnings call as the iPhone maker's CEO—in the context of a tech selloff to close last week.

Ternus took the top job shortly after Apple had its strongest June-to-August quarter. He oversaw the release of new phone and watch models this September, as well as last month's launch of a foldable iPhone that has reportedly been prone to cracking.

How much momentum the AI buildout still has may become clearer as companies that produce servers, chips and other components for data centers publish their latest quarterly results. Companies slated to report this week include Supermicro, Advanced Micro Devices, Onsemi, Arm Holdings and Lumentum Holdings.

Shopify, which recently announced a partnership with Meta's Muse AI, will also hand in its numbers, as will data analytics company Palantir. Quarterly results from Uber, Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart—the latter two firms agreed to merge last week—will round out reports from the tech sector.

There's economic data to watch this week, too: October job numbers are due Friday. Job creation was weak in September, and the government downwardly revised August and July figures, suggesting the labor market may be more fragile than economists realized. Friday's report may influence whether the Central Bank increases interest rates in December, as expected.

Market Recap

The major stock indexes wrapped up October with a bruising Friday pullback. That left two of the three leading indexes with monthly losses: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3%, its biggest one-month decline since March 2025, when markets cratered amid concerns about the Trump administration's tariff policies. The S&P 500 fell 0.9% in October, while the Dow added 1.7%, recovering from a 4.3% September decline in September. For a recap of Friday's action, see our Friday markets blog.

This Week's Top Events

Here's a look at major events happening this week. TradingView publishes a more detailed calendar, but clicking the link will take you off the Investopedia site.

Monday, Nov. 2: Palantir Technologies (PLTR) is slated to release its third-quarter results after the market closes and host a live webcast at 5 p.m. ET. The company topped expectations last quarter and raised its outlook.

Monday: Apple (AAPL) is scheduled to host a conference call on its fiscal fourth-quarter results at 5 p.m. ET, with the numbers expected before then. The tech company beat expectations last quarter, but its forecast disappointed investors.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: Shopify (SHOP) is set to release its third-quarter results before the opening bell and hold a conference call at 8:30 a.m. ET. The e-commerce company handed in better-than-expected results last quarter and shared a bright outlook, sending shares soaring.

Tuesday: Super Micro Computer (SMCI) is scheduled to host a conference call on its fiscal first-quarter results at 5 p.m. ET, with the numbers expected before then. Supermicro handed in strong numbers last quarter, and its shares rose when the server company released preliminary results that outperformed prior guidance.

Tuesday: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is set to release third-quarter results after the closing bell, followed by a conference call at 5 p.m. ET. The chipmaker posted better-than-expected results last quarter, with data center sales doubling. But AMD shares fell, potentially because investors were looking for a stronger gross margin forecast. Other AI-related companies slated to report this week include Arm Holdings (ARM), Lumentum Holdings (LITE) and Onsemi (ON).

Wednesday, Nov. 4: Uber Technologies (UBER) is scheduled to hold a conference call on its third-quarter results at 8 a.m. ET, with the numbers expected earlier that day. Shares of the ride-hailing company fell when Uber reported less revenue than expected last quarter. Investors embraced Uber's recently expanded partnership with chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA) on self-driving cars. Nvidia is also working with Lyft (LYFT), which reports Thursday.

Wednesday: McDonald's (MCD) is slated to host a conference call on its third-quarter results at 8:30 a.m. ET, with the figures expected before then. The fast-food giant reported more profit than expected last quarter. Several other restaurant chains report this week, including: Cava (CAVA), Sweetgreen (SG), Papa John's (PZZA), Shake Shack (SHAK), Wendy's (WEN)—which is weighing a buy-out offer, Texas Roadhouse (TXRH), Taco Bell owner Yum! Brands (YUM), and Bloomin' Brands (BLMN), which operates Outback Steakhouse.

Wednesday: The Kraft Heinz Co. (KHC) is scheduled to release its third-quarter results before the opening bell, followed by a live question-and-answer session at 9 a.m. ET. The company said earlier this year that it was abandoning plans to divide the business into two companies: one for sauces and spreads and another focused on grocery products. Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) also reports this week.

Wednesday: DoorDash (DASH) is slated to publish its third-quarter results after the market closes and hold a conference call at 4:30 p.m. ET. The company last week agreed to merge with rival Instacart (CART), which also reports in the coming days.

Wednesday: Snap (SNAP) is scheduled to hold a conference call on its third-quarter results at 5 p.m. ET, with the figures expected before then.

Thursday, Nov. 5: Cloudflare (NET) is set to publish its third-quarter results after the closing bell and host a conference call at 5 p.m. ET. The cloud company outperformed expectations last quarter and lifted its outlook.

Friday, Nov. 6: The Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release October job numbers at 8:30 a.m. ET. Employers added fewer jobs than expected—some 29,000—in September, and government economists said the country may have added 60,000 fewer jobs than previously believed in July and August. The unemployment rate increased to 4.2% from 4.1% in August.

Friday: The University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers is slated to release November consumer sentiment and expectation data at 10 a.m. ET. Consumer sentiment ticked down in October, remaining 15% below where it was before the conflict with Iran began.

Friday: Moderna (MRNA) is set to hold a conference call on its third-quarter results at 8 a.m. ET, with the numbers expected before then. The pharmaceutical company's stock was up nearly 700% for the year until results from its skin cancer vaccine trial were leaked, spurring a 20% drop in share prices. Other pharmaceutical and health insurance companies reporting this week include Novo Nordisk A/S (NVO), Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX), Humana (HUM) and Cigna Group (CI).
